extracted.intended_audience: geologists, archaeologists, and scientifically literate readers interested in glacial geology and palaeolithic archaeology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of geological evidence used to determine whether palaeolithic implements and extinct mammal remains are preglacial or post-glacial, based on stratigraphy, preservation, and field sections. Applies to interpreting valley-gravels, cave-deposits, and relations to glacial (bowlder-) clay in the British Isles and comparable contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to bowlder-clay (stratigraphic superposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever the relation of beds containing mammoth, woolly rhinoceros, and palaeolithic implements to the bowlder-clay can be clearly seen, they are of distinctly older age when they underlie the bowlder-clay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If remains lie below glacial clay (bowlder-clay) or the cave-deposits lie beneath glacial clay, this indicates a preglacial age. Check clear field exposures showing the contact; use this as a primary stratigraphic criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: State of preservation: worn/rolled vs uninjured
rubrics_metrics.description: Bones and flint implements found within valley-gravels are often broken and worn (rounded by rolling), whereas those found below the gravels (in situ on an old land-surface) are uninjured and sharp-edged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the degree of rounding and edge-wear to infer transport and reworking: rolled/broken specimens indicate deposition within gravels (likely transported), uninjured specimens in situ beneath gravels indicate older, primary deposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-occurrence with extinct megafauna (association in same stratum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The implements of palaeolithic man are often found together with bones of mammoth and associated extinct mammals in the same stratum of cave-earth; this contemporaneity is taken as strong evidence of the same age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When implements and megafauna remains are found in the same undisturbed layer, infer contemporaneity. Use multiple cave localities and repeated association as weight for the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occurrence limited to caves in glaciated districts
rubrics_metrics.description: In glaciated parts of the country mammalian remains are found only where preserved from the action of the ice in caverns and fissures; they are absent in valley-gravels of glaciated districts except in such protected contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of remains in open glaciated valley-gravels (but presence in caves beneath glacial deposits) supports preglacial age for those remains; interpret absence/presence in relation to glacial coverage and preservation potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative position on valley slopes (higher vs lower horizons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Palaeolithic implements are generally found higher up the slopes of valleys than the mammalian remains; this may reflect humans frequenting more elevated, drier localities than the large mammals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider micro-topographic distribution within valley systems when interpreting contemporaneity and depositional processes; vertical/horizontal relationships within terrace/gravel sequences inform behavioral and taphonomic inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field-section verification of theoretical diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical stratigraphic diagrams (e.g., showing implement-bearing beds in a trough cut in bowlder-clay) must be checked against actual observed sections and facts in the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept schematic sections as proof; verify with measured exposures and multiple localities. Prestwich's theoretical section at Hoxne is cited as requiring checking against observed data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of human bones beneath glacial clay (direct evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of human remains (e.g., a human fibula) in cave-deposits that lie beneath glacial clay provides direct evidence for preglacial human presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use directly datable or diagnostic human skeletal remains found stratigraphically below glacial deposits as strong evidence; corroborate with the stratigraphic context and associated fauna.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character and persistence of specific beds (e.g., the 'trail')
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistent beds such as the upper 'trail' (a sandy bed with stones) that cap lowland gravels across regions are important markers in interpreting glacial sequences and the relative age of underlying deposits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map and trace regionally persistent beds as stratigraphic markers; their occurrence above or below implement-bearing gravels affects age interpretations. Note variation (e.g., 'trail' vs upper bowlder-clay) across sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pebble/clast provenance and fabric
rubrics_metrics.description: The composition of gravels (e.g., presence of chalk pebbles in lowest beds, stones derived from other sources, angular patches) and sedimentary structures (false-bedding, lenticular beds) are diagnostic of depositional processes involved in spreading gravels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse clast types, angularity, and bedding to infer transport mechanisms (e.g., debacle/flood vs glacial deposition). Irregular bases, nests of flints, and derived stones indicate reworking or complex deposition histories to be accounted for in age interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of widespread gravel outspread hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal that outspread of valley-gravels was due to a great flood or débâcle (e.g., from breaking an ice-barrier in the English Channel) is offered as an explanatory model for how gravels containing implements and mammal remains were deposited preglacially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider regional depositional models (flood/débâcle vs glacial processes) when explaining the stratigraphic position of remains; evaluate the model against field evidence such as sediment character, sorting, and stratigraphic relationships.
